- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–2% to account for mean reversion or hidden support.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in the following 5–7 days; apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 1–3% from forecast for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model often fails to adjust; check for lagged sentiment reversal and adjust forecast downward by 1–3% in next 2–3 periods.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently overestimates in early periods (days 1–7) when sentiment is volatile; apply a “volatility dampener” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% for first 7 days if sentiment is mixed or trending.
- If sentiment is consistently 0.00 or negative, model underestimates; add a “sentiment floor” — forecast should not fall below 10–15% below recent 7-day low unless confirmed by technical support.
- When sentiment is high and price is near 30-day high, model often overcorrects downward; apply a “high-sentiment ceiling” — cap forecast at 10–15% above recent high if sentiment remains strong.
